1093.title: Gifts of the Spirit (1 Corinthians 12)
1093.hook: wisdom, knowledge, faith, healing, tongues: one Spirit, many gifts, one body
1093.howItsDone: Christians read 1 Corinthians 12 as teaching that each member of the church has gifts for the good of all; Pentecostal and charismatic churches expect gifts like healing, prophecy and tongues in worship, and Catholic teaching speaks of many kinds of charisms, including those of religious orders.

segments.voice: Yesterday, sanctification: set apart, then slowly grown into love. Your line was perfect in love.

A letter is being read aloud to a church in Corinth, and the room is tense. Paul has heard things. Some there have spectacular gifts and seem to know it. Others feel they bring nothing. So Paul writes a strange, mixed list: a word of wisdom, a word of knowledge, faith, healing, miracles, prophecy, telling spirits apart, tongues, and the interpreting of tongues. Some sound quiet and some sound loud. And like a drumbeat he repeats one phrase: by the same Spirit. To one this, by the same Spirit. To another that. In this list he isn't ranking anyone. He's tying the whole room together.

Charism is the church's word for a gift of the Spirit: given not as a prize, but for someone else's good. Day two hundred ninety-five met the Pentecostal side of these gifts; today, Paul's chapter itself. It opens, in the King James: "Now there are diversities of gifts, but the same Spirit." And why they're given: "the manifestation of the Spirit is given to every man to profit withal." For the common good. A gift that only makes its owner look impressive has missed the point. Then Paul reaches for a body. A foot might say, I'm not a hand, so I'm not part of this. An ear might say, I'm not an eye. If the whole body were an eye, where would the hearing be? Then the line that turns the room around: "the eye cannot say unto the hand, I have no need of thee." The parts that "seem to be more feeble, are necessary." Not tolerated. Necessary. Christians read this chapter differently. Pentecostal and charismatic churches give great weight to the gifts that show, like healing, prophecy and tongues, and expect them in worship today. Catholic teaching uses charism broadly, for gifts as quiet as teaching or care for the sick, and speaks of whole religious orders having their own charism. Other churches stress gifts like leading, giving and encouraging, which Paul names in Romans. Underneath sits Paul's picture: many gifts, one Spirit, one body. And notice what comes right after this chapter. It's the one about love.

segments.voice: Bring to mind one person, at church, at work or at home, and skip their obvious talents; look for the quiet gift, like noticing who's left out, or calming a room. Give that gift a name in a few plain words, and sit with the thought that the people around them need it. If you pray, give thanks for that person by name; if you don't, just hold their gift in mind.
Charism. A gift of the Spirit, given for the good of others, one of many in one body.
Your line: many gifts, one spirit. The feeble parts are necessary. I'll be here tomorrow.

1094.title: The fruit of the Spirit (Galatians 5:22–23)
1094.hook: love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, self-control
1094.howItsDone: Some Christians memorize the fruit of the Spirit from Galatians 5:22–23 and use the list to examine their lives.

segments.voice: Yesterday, charism: a gift of the Spirit, given for someone else's good. Your line was many gifts, one spirit.

Nobody has ever heard an apple tree grunt. It doesn't clench its branches in spring and force the apples out. It stands in the sun, drinks the rain, stays rooted, and one day the fruit is just there. A gardener can water, prune and wait. A gardener can't make an apple. Yesterday Paul listed gifts: to one person this, to another that. Now he writes to different churches, the churches of Galatia, and the picture changes from a toolbox to an orchard.

Here's the verse in the King James: "But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, longsuffering, gentleness, goodness, faith, Meekness, temperance: against such there is no law." Look at the first words. The fruit is. Not the fruits are. One fruit, many flavors. Some readers hear one life growing all of these together, not a menu where you pick a favorite. Set that beside yesterday. Gifts are handed out differently: one person heals, another teaches. Some readers add that the fruit is meant for everyone: nobody is let off love because their gift is administration. Just before, Paul lists what he calls "the works of the flesh." Works on one side, fruit on the other. Works are made. Fruit grows. Then the old words. Longsuffering is patience that holds out a long time. Faith, here, is faithfulness. Meekness is gentleness, strength that doesn't push. Temperance is self-control. In today's English, it sounds like someone you'd want to live next door to. So is there no effort at all? Christians answer that differently. The same chapter says, "Walk in the Spirit." Walking takes steps. Jesus, in John's Gospel, says: "I am the vine, ye are the branches," and the branch bears fruit by staying joined to the vine. Prayer, worship, scripture, sacraments, serving others: in Christian teaching these keep the branch joined, like sun and rain. They don't manufacture fruit. And "against such there is no law" has a smile in it. Try picturing a court that bans patience.

Don't plan to squeeze it out of yourself; picture one moment where it could grow, a long line, a slow reply, a hard conversation. If you pray, ask for that fruit by name; if you don't, keep the one word with you, like a seed in a pocket.
The fruit of the Spirit. One fruit with many flavors, grown, not manufactured: love, joy, peace, and the rest.

1095.title: Tongues, then and now
1095.hook: Pentecostals and charismatics pray in tongues; some Christians believe such gifts ceased, others are open
1095.howItsDone: Pentecostal and charismatic Christians pray in tongues privately and in worship, often with interpretation; Christians in some Reformed and Baptist churches believe such gifts ceased with the apostles, and others are open to the gift while stressing Paul's rules for order.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the fruit of the Spirit: one fruit, many flavors, grown rather than forced. Your line was fruit, not effort.

What does it sound like? In a Pentecostal service the music softens, and around the room people begin to pray aloud, but not in words the visitor next to them can follow. Syllables rise and fall, like a language overheard through a wall. For the people praying, this is a gift of the Spirit. Across town, a pastor teaches that gifts like this belonged to the apostles' time and have ceased. In a third church, people say kindly that they're open, but cautious. Same Bible, three answers.

It starts at Pentecost, in Acts; day one thousand forty-one saw churches wear red for it. A sound like a rushing wind, and "they were all filled with the Holy Ghost, and began to speak with other tongues, as the Spirit gave them utterance." Here the crowd understands: visitors from many lands each hear their own language. Corinth seems different. Paul writes that "he that speaketh in an unknown tongue speaketh not unto men, but unto God." Nobody understands without an interpreter. So Paul sets rules: two or three, one at a time, and with no interpreter, keep silent in the church and speak to God privately. And a balance: "covet to prophesy, and forbid not to speak with tongues." Three answers come out of these pages. Pentecostal and charismatic Christians pray in tongues today, often as a private prayer language, sometimes aloud in worship with interpretation; some Pentecostal churches teach it as the sign of being baptized in the Spirit. Cessationists, in some Reformed and Baptist churches, read the gifts as signs that confirmed the apostles' message and ceased with that age; they point to Paul: "whether there be tongues, they shall cease." Pentecostals answer that the passage puts the ceasing when "that which is perfect is come," which they read as Christ's return. Others sit between: open to the gift, wary of pressure, glad of Paul's rules for order. Each side takes the same chapters seriously. Some Christians reach for John's line: "The wind bloweth where it listeth." In that reading, the Spirit isn't on a leash, in anybody's church.

If you pray, ask for humility toward those who pray differently; if you don't, simply breathe, and let the wind be the wind.
Tongues. Speech given by the Spirit: languages heard at Pentecost, prayer unto God in Corinth, and a question the churches still answer differently.
Your line: the spirit blows. Same Bible, three answers, all taken seriously. See you tomorrow.

1096.title: Four marks
1096.hook: the church is one, holy, catholic and apostolic, each tradition explaining how
1096.howItsDone: Catholic, Orthodox, Anglican, Lutheran and other churches confess the church as one, holy, catholic and apostolic in the Nicene Creed, often aloud together at the Eucharist; each tradition explains the marks in its own way.

segments.voice: Yesterday, tongues, and three answers from one Bible. Your line was the spirit blows.

This Sunday, in a Catholic parish, an Orthodox cathedral and an Anglican chapel, people will stand and say the same old sentence from the Nicene Creed. It describes the church in four words: one, holy, catholic, apostolic. Then they'll go home to churches that are plainly not one, sometimes not holy, very local, and arguing about what the apostles meant. So what are they saying? A wish? A boast? A promise? These four words are the marks of the church: the signs you're meant to recognize it by. Day three hundred six met the small-c catholic. Today, all four.
screen: `A WISH, A BOAST, OR A PROMISE?`

segments.voice: One at a time. One. Paul writes to the Ephesians: "There is one body, and one Spirit, even as ye are called in one hope of your calling; One Lord, one faith, one baptism." And in John's Gospel Jesus prays "That they all may be one." Holy. Not because its members are spotless, but because it belongs to God, set apart. Catholic, small c: universal, for the whole, every place, every people, the whole faith. Apostolic. Paul says the household of God is "built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets, Jesus Christ himself being the chief corner stone." Now the explanations, side by side. The Catholic Church teaches that the one church of Christ subsists in the Catholic Church, apostolic through bishops in succession from the apostles, in communion with the pope, while recognizing real elements of the church beyond its walls. The Orthodox Church holds that it is the one church, kept apostolic by bishops who guard the faith handed down. Anglicans also keep bishops in succession and see themselves within the one catholic church. Protestant confessions like Augsburg find the church wherever the gospel is rightly preached and the sacraments rightly given; apostolic, for them, means teaching what the apostles taught. So the same words can describe a visible body with a shape and a history, or a fellowship of believers spread through many churches. One thing these explanations can share: the marks are said as faith, not as a report card. Christians say them on days when their own church looks nothing like them.

Four marks. One, holy, catholic and apostolic: the signs of the church in the Nicene Creed, said together, explained differently.

1097.title: Who decides?
1097.hook: a pope, councils of bishops, synods, or congregations: churches order authority differently
1097.howItsDone: Catholics are led by the pope and bishops, Orthodox churches by bishops in synods, Presbyterian and Reformed churches by elders in sessions and assemblies, and Baptist and other congregational churches by the gathered members; churches often pray for their leaders by name in worship.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the four marks: one, holy, catholic, apostolic, said together and explained differently.

The argument has traveled all the way from Antioch to Jerusalem. The church is young; the question is big: must believers who aren't Jewish take on the whole law of Moses, circumcision included, to follow Jesus? Good people stand on both sides. So, in the fifteenth chapter of Acts, the apostles and elders come together. There's much disputing. Peter tells what he's seen. Paul and Barnabas tell their stories. Then James gives his judgment. And the letter they send out carries a sentence worth hearing slowly. Behind it sits today's question: who decides?

The letter says: "For it seemed good to the Holy Ghost, and to us." Both: the Spirit, and a room of people who argued. Churches across the traditions hold that hope: that their decisions can be human and holy at once. But they've built that room very differently. Catholics look to the pope, the bishop of Rome, as Peter's successor, with the bishops in communion with him; they read Jesus's words, "thou art Peter, and upon this rock I will build my church," as founding that office. The Orthodox are governed by bishops in councils and synods, with patriarchs who lead without a single head over all, and see the council in Acts as their pattern. Presbyterian and Reformed churches are led by elders, ruling together in local sessions and wider assemblies; they point to the elders in that chapter. Baptists and other congregational churches gather the members to decide, trusting the Spirit to speak through the whole body, and notice that the apostles and elders acted with "the whole church." Each can read Acts fifteen and see its own room. Under it all sits something Jesus said when two disciples asked for the best seats and the others were angry. Rulers lord it over people. "But so shall it not be among you: but whosoever will be great among you, shall be your minister." A minister, in that old English, is a servant. Paul adds: "Let all things be done decently and in order." In Christian teaching, order is meant to serve love: so the hungry get fed, the gospel gets told, and nobody gets trampled.

1098.title: Ministers
1098.hook: bishops, priests, deacons, pastors, elders; churches differ on ordaining women, some do and some don't
1098.howItsDone: In churches across traditions a person is ordained in a service of prayer with the laying on of hands, by a bishop in Catholic, Orthodox and Anglican churches, or by ministers and elders in other Protestant churches; churches differ on whether women may be ordained.

segments.voice: Yesterday, who decides: popes and bishops, synods, elders, whole congregations. Your line was order for love.

The problem was the food line. In the sixth chapter of Acts, the church in Jerusalem shares meals with widows every day, and the Greek-speaking believers complain that their widows are being overlooked. The apostles can't preach and run the kitchen too. So the church chooses seven men, of honest report, full of the Holy Ghost and wisdom, to see that the food is shared fairly. Then a small, physical moment churches still repeat: "when they had prayed, they laid their hands on them." Hands on heads, to send people out to serve tables.

Ordination is the church setting someone apart for a ministry, usually with prayer and the laying on of hands. Paul reminds Timothy of it: "Neglect not the gift that is in thee, which was given thee by prophecy, with the laying on of the hands of the presbytery." A gift given through other people's hands. And the first hands in Acts weren't for a throne. They were for a kitchen. The titles vary. Catholic, Orthodox and Anglican churches ordain bishops, priests and deacons. Catholics and the Orthodox count holy orders as a sacrament, and Catholic teaching says it leaves a lasting mark on the person ordained. Lutheran, Reformed, Methodist and Baptist churches ordain pastors, ministers, elders and deacons, and often describe ordination as the church recognizing and confirming a call God has already given. And here churches differ in a way that matters deeply to people on every side: whether women may be ordained. The Catholic and Orthodox churches ordain only men as priests and bishops, holding that they follow Christ's own choice of apostles. Some Protestant and Anglican churches ordain women as pastors, priests and bishops, pointing to women like Phebe, whom Paul calls "a servant of the church which is at Cenchrea." Other Protestant churches, including some Baptist and Reformed ones, ordain only men as pastors, reading Paul's letters to Timothy as setting that pattern. Traditions differ, and each side reads scripture seriously and holds its answer with care. What these ordinations share is in that first scene: hands, prayer, and a job to do for others.

1099.title: Priesthood of all believers
1099.hook: Luther stressed that every baptized Christian has a priestly calling (1 Peter 2:9)
1099.howItsDone: Protestant churches teach the priesthood of all believers, often with a strong sense of ordinary work as a calling; Catholic teaching speaks of the common priesthood of the baptized alongside the ordained priesthood, and Orthodox Christians speak of the royal priesthood of the whole people of God.

segments.voice: Yesterday, ordination: hands and prayer, setting people apart to serve. Your line was called to serve.

A cobbler bends over a shoe, stitching by lamplight. A blacksmith sweats at his forge. A farmer walks behind a plow. In Martin Luther's Germany, people spoke of a spiritual estate, the priests and monks, and a worldly estate, everyone else. Luther disagreed, loudly. In a letter to the German nobility, he wrote that the cobbler, the smith and the farmer each have the work of their trade, and yet all of them, by baptism, are alike consecrated priests. Not just the priest at the altar. The cobbler too. He found it in a much older letter.

That older letter is the first letter of Peter: "But ye are a chosen generation, a royal priesthood, an holy nation, a peculiar people." Written to ordinary believers, not clergy. And Peter echoes a far older promise at Mount Sinai, where God tells Israel, "ye shall be unto me a kingdom of priests, and an holy nation." Jews read that verse as their own calling, and Peter's readers heard themselves invited into its language. So what does a priest do? A priest stands between: bringing people's needs to God, and God's blessing to people. Peter says this whole people exists to "shew forth the praises of him who hath called you out of darkness into his marvellous light." Luther pressed it hard. If every baptized person is a priest, no one stands higher before God because of their job. A pastor still serves, for good order, as we saw yesterday. But a mother changing diapers and a monk saying his prayers stand on the same ground. Protestant teachers built on it a high view of ordinary work as a calling. Other churches read the verse their own way. Catholic teaching speaks of a common priesthood shared by all the baptized, and a ministerial priesthood of the ordained, different in kind, yet ordered to one another. Orthodox Christians speak of the royal priesthood of the whole people of God, offering the world back to God in thanksgiving. And a line from Paul for any workbench: "whatsoever ye do, do it heartily, as to the Lord, and not unto men."
